title: The cat demon
translation: "Deep in the mountains," people said, "there's a thing called a cat demon, and it eats people." Someone else said, "Not just in the mountains. Even around here, cats get old, turn into cat demons and carry people off."
A priest called Something-amidabutsu, who lived near Gyōganji and was keen on linked verse, heard this. "If you go about on your own," he thought, "you'd better watch out."

Right around then, he was at a linked-verse party somewhere until late at night and walked home alone. On the bank of a little stream, there it was, the cat demon he had heard about. It came straight for his feet, jumped up at him, and went for his throat.
All his nerve was gone. He tried to fight it off, but he had no strength, his legs gave way, and he tumbled into the stream. "Help! Cat demon! Help! Help!"

People came running out of the houses with torches, and found a priest they all knew from the neighbourhood. "What on earth?" They pulled him up out of the water. The prizes he had won at the party, a fan and a little box, had been tucked in his robe, and they were soaked. He looked like a man who had escaped death by a miracle, and he crawled into his house on all fours.
It was his own dog, apparently. It knew its master even in the dark, and had jumped up at him.

literal: When people said, 'In the deep mountains there is a thing called a nekomata, and it eats people, they say',
there was someone who said, 'Even though it is not the mountains, around here too, cats grow old and become nekomata and take people, I hear', and
a priest called Something-amidabutsu, who composed linked verse and lived near Gyōganji, heard this and thought, 'One who walks about alone should be careful'; just at that time,

he composed linked verse somewhere until late at night and was returning all alone, when on the bank of a stream the nekomata he had heard of came suddenly, without fail, to his feet, and at once, clinging to him, tried to eat at his neck.
His wits gone, he had no strength to fend it off, his legs gave way, he tumbled into the stream and shouted, 'Help! Nekomata! Help, help!', and
from the houses people lit torches, ran up and looked, and it was a priest they knew from the neighbourhood.

Saying 'What is this?', they lifted him up out of the river, and the prizes he had won at linked verse, a fan, a small box and the like, which he had in the fold of his robe, had gone into the water too.
Looking as if he had been saved by a rare chance, he crawled into his house.
It was the dog he kept, which knew its master though it was dark and had jumped on him, they say.

notes.text: {猫|ねこ}また: a cat that has lived so long it turns into a monster. The name is usually explained as 'forked': in later pictures the nekomata has a tail split in two. Fujiwara no Teika's diary already reports one killing people around Nara in 1233, a century before Kenkō.
なり after the plain form of a verb means hearsay: 'it eats people, they say'. あなる in the next sentence is the same: ある + なる, 'there are, I hear'. Everyone in the opening has only heard about it.

'Something-amidabutsu, or whatever it was'. Pure Land priests and lay believers often took names ending in -amidabutsu (later shortened to -ami). とかや: 'or something like that'. Kenkō gives the name only vaguely.

{行願寺|ぎやうぐわんじ}: a temple in Kyoto, better known as Kōdō. In Kenkō's time it stood in the north of the city, near Ichijō. The {小川|をがは} where the priest falls is probably the Ogawa, a small stream that ran past it.

{連歌|れんが}: linked verse. Several people take turns adding lines to one long chain of verses. In Kenkō's day it was hugely popular, and sessions were often played for prizes ({賭物|かけもの}) and ran late into the night.
'Without fail, unmistakably': it went straight for him, just as the stories said it would.

notes.quote: 希有にして助かりたるさまにて
notes.text: {希有|けう}: 'rare, extraordinary'. He looked like someone saved by a miracle. Modern けう 'rare' is the same word.
'Crawling'. Modern ほうほうの{体|てい}, 'in a sorry state, scrambling away', comes from this.

notes.quote: 飛びつきたりけるとぞ
notes.text: とぞ: 'so they say', with the rest of the sentence left out. The explanation comes only in the last line, after the whole fright, and the story ends there.
